title: Salivary glands
description: Diseases of the major (parotid, submandibular, sublingual) and minor salivary glands — obstructive, infective, inflammatory, autoimmune, and neoplastic.

problems.description: Recurrent episodic unilateral parotid pain and swelling provoked by eating, relieved between meals.
problems.etiology: A calculus forms within the parotid duct, obstructing salivary outflow. The obstruction is most often detected on plain radiographs, though a significant proportion of calculi are radiolucent [1]. Sialography can reveal a stricture or complete obstruction even when plain films appear normal [2].
problems.presentation: Pain and swelling of the parotid arise characteristically before and during meals, when salivary flow is stimulated against the obstructed duct [1]. The pattern is episodic and recurrent. The overlying skin and gland feel tense during an episode.
problems.results: Plain X-rays of the cheek reveal radio-opaque calculi [1]. Sialography demonstrates a stricture or filling defect at the obstruction site [2]. Sialoendoscopy with laser lithotripsy is available in specialist centres for proximal calculi under 3 mm in patients wishing to avoid surgery [3].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Eating-triggered episodic parotid swelling that resolves between meals is the hallmark [1]. The parotid location distinguishes this from submandibular sialolithiasis, which is the commoner site overall and presents in the floor of mouth [1].
problems.treatment: Anterior parotid duct calculi can be exposed via an intraoral approach and lifted out directly; more posterior calculi require a small skin flap over a probe placed in the duct [4]. Selective superficial parotidectomy is the only safe approach for deep or inaccessible stones [4]. Sialoendoscopy with laser lithotripsy is a conservative alternative for small proximal calculi [3].
problems.prognosis: Removal of the obstructing calculus resolves the episodic swelling. Persistent or recurrent obstruction leading to sialectasis may ultimately require gland excision [5].

citations.quote: History is of recurrent pain and swelling in the obstructed gland, particularly before and during meals. Plain X-rays (lower occlusal for submandibular, cheek for parotid) reveal radio-opaque calculi, but do not exclude the radiolucent calculi and mucous plugs.
Sialography reveals a stricture or obstruction.
Sialoendoscopy ± laser lithotripsy is available in some centres for proximal calculi in patients wishing to avoid gland excision and calculi <3mm.

Rx: parotid duct—expose duct via IO approach for anterior stones or via a small skin flap onto a probe in the duct for more posterior calculi. Otherwise, selective superficial parotidectomy is the only safe approach.
Severe recurrent infection of the parotid or submandibular glands leads to dilatation and ballooning of the ducts and alveoli called sialectasis.

problems.description: Painful unilateral major salivary gland swelling with purulent discharge from the duct opening.
problems.etiology: Acute bacterial sialadenitis arises from ascending infection, commonly via duct obstruction or systemic dehydration in elderly patients [1]. Common infecting organisms are oral streptococci, oral anaerobes, and Staphylococcus aureus [1]. Chronic bacterial sialadenitis often exists as a complication of duct obstruction and can flare as an acute exacerbation [1].
problems.presentation: A painful swelling of the affected major gland, almost always unilateral, with purulent discharge expressible from the duct orifice [1]. Ascending parotid infection is a recognised presentation in dehydrated elderly inpatients [1].
problems.results: Plain radiographs may reveal an obstructing calculus, though 50% are radiolucent [1]. Culture of pus from the duct identifies the causative organism [1]. Ultrasound can localise a loculated pus collection within the gland if incision and drainage is being considered [1]. Once acute symptoms resolve, sialography is indicated to define duct structure [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Unilateral painful gland swelling with expressible pus from the duct is the diagnostic picture [1]. Both acute and chronic forms are almost always unilateral [1].
problems.treatment: Rehydration and exclusion or removal of any obstructing calculus are the first steps [1]. Aggressive antibiotic therapy with co-amoxiclav, or amoxicillin combined with metronidazole, covers the typical organisms [1]. Stimulation of salivary flow by chewing or massage helps chronic recurring disease [1]. Rarely, loculated pus necessitates incision and drainage [1]. Recurrent chronic sialadenitis unresponsive to conservative measures is an indication for gland removal [2].
problems.prognosis: Most acute episodes resolve with rehydration, antibiotics, and management of any obstruction. Recurrent chronic sialadenitis can lead to sialectasis and may ultimately require gland excision [2].

citations.quote: Acute bacterial sialadenitis presents as a painful swelling, usually with a purulent discharge from the duct of the gland involved. It may also develop as an exacerbation of chronic bacterial sialadenitis, which often exists as a complication of duct obstruction. Ascending infection of the parotid glands occurs in dehydrated elderly patients. Both acute and chronic conditions are almost always unilateral and common infecting organisms are oral streptococci, oral anaerobes, and Staphylococcus aureus. Rx: rehydration and exclusion or removal of an obstructing calculus. Plain radiographs may reveal calculus, but 50% are radiolucent. Culture of pus from the duct and aggressive antibiotic therapy (co-amoxiclav or amoxicillin and metronidazole). Stimulation of salivary flow by chewing or massage helps chronic recurring sialadenitis. Rarely, loculated pus collection within the gland necessitates incision and drainage; USS can localize collection. Once the acute symptoms have resolved, sialography is indicated to define duct structure and may prove therapeutic.
Recurrent chronic sialadenitis is an indication for removal of the gland.

problems.description: Acute bilateral parotid swelling with fever in a child or young adult; may have orchitis or meningitis in adults.
problems.etiology: Mumps is an acute infectious paramyxoviral disease transmitted by direct contact with droplets of saliva [1]. It primarily affects the parotid glands (10% also involve the submandibular gland) [1]. Protection is conferred by the MMR vaccine, though UK incidence has risen following reduced vaccine uptake secondary to fraudulent but widely publicised research [1].
problems.presentation: Sudden onset of fever, pain, and parotid swelling [1]. Classically one gland is affected first, although bilateral swelling is the norm [1]. Usually affects children and young adults [1]. In adults the disease is more severe, with multisystem complications including epididymo-orchitis, oophoritis, mastitis, pancreatitis, thyroiditis, and meningoencephalitis [1].
problems.results: Diagnosis is clinical. The bilateral parotid distribution, fever, and epidemiological context (unvaccinated individual or outbreak) are the key pointers. Serology can confirm acutely rising antibody titres to the mumps virus.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Bilateral parotid swelling in an unvaccinated child or young adult, with fever and an epidemiological context, is the hallmark [1]. The adult multisystem complications — particularly orchitis and meningitis — distinguish this from bacterial sialadenitis [1].
problems.treatment: Management is supportive. The patient should be isolated for 7–10 days to limit transmission [1].
problems.prognosis: Self-limiting in the majority. Adult men carry a risk of epididymo-orchitis, which can in rare cases affect fertility. Meningoencephalitis is the most serious complication. MMR vaccination is highly effective at preventing the disease [1].

citations.quote: Viral sialadenitis, commonly mumps, is an acute, infectious paramyxoviral disease which primarily affects the parotid (10% submandibular gland). It is transmitted by direct contact with droplets of saliva and usually affects children and young adults with sudden onset of fever, pain, and parotid swelling. Classically, one gland is affected first, although bilateral swelling is the norm. In adults, the disease is more severe, with multisystem problems such as epididymo-orchitis, oophoritis/mastitis, pancreatitis, thyroiditis, and meningoencephalitis. Protection is conferred by the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine, however the incidence in the UK has ↑ following reduced vaccine intake 2° to fraudulent but highly publicized 'research'. Rx: supportive, isolate patient for 7–10 days.

problems.description: Dry mouth and dry eyes in a middle-aged woman, often alongside joint disease; raised risk of salivary lymphoma.
problems.etiology: An autoimmune disease affecting salivary and lacrimal glands, causing a reduction in secretory activity [1]. About 90% of patients are female [1]. Secondary Sjögren syndrome comprises the triad of xerostomia, keratoconjunctivitis sicca, and a connective tissue disorder — most commonly rheumatoid arthritis, but sometimes SLE, systemic sclerosis, or primary biliary cholangitis [1, 2]. When the connective tissue component is absent, the condition is termed primary Sjögren syndrome (sicca syndrome) [1]. There is a 5% risk of malignant lymphomatous transformation of the affected gland [1].
problems.presentation: Dry mouth and dry eyes are the cardinal symptoms [1, 3]. Actual swelling of the salivary glands is relatively uncommon; late-onset parotid swelling may herald lymphoma [2]. Systemic features of the associated connective tissue disease are present in secondary Sjögren syndrome [2].
problems.results: Antinuclear antibodies are positive in 70%, SSA in 70%, SSB in 40%, and rheumatoid factor in 70%. ESR and immunoglobulins are elevated [1]. Labial gland biopsy may show a lymphocytic infiltrate [1]. Saliva flowmetry, sialography, Schirmer test, and slit-lamp examination can all be performed [1]. Diagnosis requires four positive findings from six categories: ocular symptoms, oral symptoms, ocular signs, histopathological features, salivary gland involvement, and autoantibodies [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The combination of xerostomia, keratoconjunctivitis sicca, and positive autoantibodies (SSA/SSB) in a woman with rheumatoid arthritis or other connective tissue disease is the classic picture [1]. The 5% lymphoma risk mandates long-term monitoring [1].
problems.treatment: Management is symptomatic: synthetic saliva, synthetic tears, meticulous oral hygiene, and treatment of oral candida [1]. Patients need to be made aware of the risk of lymphomatous change [1]. In severe cases, corticosteroids and immunosuppressive drugs may be required [1].
problems.prognosis: No curative treatment exists. The dry eye and dry mouth are managed long-term symptomatically. The principal concern is the approximately 5% risk of malignant lymphoma arising in the affected glands, requiring lifelong surveillance [1].

citations.quote: About 90% of patients with Sjögren syndrome are female. It comprises the triad of xerostomia, keratoconjunctivitis sicca, and a connective tissue disorder, usually rheumatoid arthritis. When the connective tissue component is absent the condition is called primary Sjögren syndrome (sicca syndrome). This is an autoimmune disease affecting salivary and lacrimal glands and causing a reduction of the secretion activity. The aetiology is probably autoimmune and there is a 5% risk of malignant lymphomatous transformation of the affected gland. ∆: antinuclear antibodies (70% +ve), SSA (70% +ve), SSB (40% +ve). Rheumatoid factor (70% +ve), ESR (i), immunoglobulins (i), labial gland biopsy may show lymphocytic infiltrate. Saliva flowmetry, sialography, Schirmer test, and slit lamp exam can be performed. Diagnosis is made on the basis of four positive findings out of the six categories which include ocular symptoms, oral symptoms, ocular signs, histopathological features, salivary gland involvement, and autoantibodies. Management is symptomatic Rx which may include synthetic saliva, synthetic tears, meticulous OH, Rx of candida, and patient awareness of the risk of lymphomatous change.

In addition to dry eyes and dry mouth this has both the serology and symptomatology of an autoimmune condition, usually rheumatoid arthritis, but sometimes SLE, systemic sclerosis, or 1° biliary cholangitis. Actual swelling of the salivary glands is relatively uncommon and late-onset swelling of the parotids may herald the presence of a lymphoma.
Xerostomia and keratoconjunctivitis sicca, i.e. dry mouth and dry eyes. There is an ↑ risk of developing parotid lymphoma with this condition.

problems.description: Firm slow-growing swelling in the parotid region, present for years, with no pain or nerve involvement.
problems.etiology: The commonest benign salivary tumour. About 80% of all salivary tumours are benign, 80% occur in the parotid, and 80% of those are in the superficial lobe [1]. Pleomorphic salivary adenomas have a mixed cellular appearance on histopathology and are the majority of this group [1]. Although benign, satellite cells may lie outside the tumour capsule, creating a propensity for recurrence if the tumour is simply enucleated [1].
problems.presentation: A firm, slow-growing parotid swelling. A long history without pain and without facial nerve involvement strongly suggests a benign tumour [2]. Fixation to surrounding tissues, pain, facial nerve involvement, rapid growth, size over 4 cm, and lymphadenopathy all point toward malignancy [1, 2].
problems.results: CT, fine-needle aspiration cytology, ultrasound, and MRI may assist characterisation [2]. History and examination remain the prime diagnostic tools [2]. The chance of malignancy is much greater in tumours over 4 cm [2].
problems.definingCharacteristics: A firm, mobile, slow-growing parotid mass in a middle-aged adult without facial nerve involvement is the classic presentation [2]. The satellite-cell biology outside the capsule means enucleation alone gives unacceptably high recurrence rates [1].
problems.treatment: A tumour in the parotid must be removed by formal parotidectomy or at minimum formal extracapsular dissection, taking a safe margin of normal tissue [1]. Simple enucleation is inadequate because of satellite cells outside the capsule [1]. The principles are complete excision with a margin of healthy tissue and preservation of the facial nerve [3].
problems.prognosis: Formal parotidectomy with a clear margin gives good long-term control. Simple enucleation carries a high recurrence risk. Malignant transformation can occur in a pre-existing pleomorphic adenoma [4].

citations.quote: About 80% are benign; 80% occur in the parotid and 80% of these are in the superficial lobe. The majority are pleomorphic salivary adenomas (PSAs) which have a mixed cellular appearance on histopathology. Although benign, the cells lie within the capsule of the tumour and satellite cells may lie outside the capsule, creating a tremendous propensity for recurrence if simply enucleated. A tumour in the parotid should therefore be removed by parotidectomy or at minimum formal extracapsular dissection, taking a safe margin of normal tissue if possible.

History and examination are the prime diagnostic tools. Long history, no pain, and no facial nerve involvement suggest benign tumour. Facial palsy, pain, and rapid growth suggest malignancy. Chance of malignancy much greater in tumours >4cm.
The principles are complete excision of a tumour with a margin of healthy tissue and preservation of facial nerve.
Other carcinomas are rare, but may arise in a pre-existing pleomorphic adenoma or de novo.

problems.description: Soft fluctuant parotid swelling in an older male smoker; may be bilateral; slow-growing and cystic in feel.
problems.etiology: Adenolymphoma (Warthin's tumour) is found almost exclusively in the parotid [1]. It affects males more than females and is rare under 50 years of age [1]. An association with smoking is well established [1].
problems.presentation: A soft and cystic-feeling swelling in the parotid region [1]. Bilateral involvement occurs in approximately 10% of cases [1]. The tumour is benign and grows slowly.
problems.results: History and examination are the prime diagnostic tools [2]. The characteristic soft, fluctuant, cystic feel is distinctive [1]. CT, fine-needle aspiration cytology, ultrasound, and MRI may be used where the diagnosis is uncertain or before extracapsular dissection is planned [2].
problems.definingCharacteristics: A soft, cystic parotid lump in an older male smoker — bilateral in 10% — is the hallmark presentation [1]. It is benign and very unlikely to recur despite being multifocal [1].
problems.treatment: Surgical excision. Because recurrence is very unlikely despite multifocality, formal parotidectomy with facial nerve preservation is the standard approach [2]. Surgery of the major salivary glands for tumours follows the principle that all salivary gland tumours, with the exception of lymphomas, should have surgery initially [3].
problems.prognosis: Benign with very low recurrence risk [1]. Malignant transformation is not a recognised feature, unlike pleomorphic adenoma.

citations.quote: Monomorphic adenoma—adenolymphoma (Warthin's tumour) affects M > F; rare <50yrs. Bilateral in 10%. Feels soft and cystic. Benign, very unlikely to recur despite being multifocal, associated with smoking.
History and examination are the prime diagnostic tools. Long history, no pain, and no facial nerve involvement suggest benign tumour.

Surgery of the major salivary glands is primarily for tumours, obstruction, and, less commonly, inflammatory conditions. With the exception of lymphomas all salivary gland tumours should have surgery initially, patient permitting.
